newsitem.title: USA: Blue-chip stocks fall again on profit-taking.
newsitem.headline: Blue-chip stocks fall again on profit-taking.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks fell for a second session Wednesday as investors took profits in big-name stocks and directed at least some of their cash to smaller issues.
At 1 p.m. EST, the Dow Jones industrial average was off 21.24 points to 6,421.45 as the market absorbed additional selling after Tuesday's 79-point loss, the biggest setback in nearly five months.
In the broader market, declining issues led advances 12-9 on active volume of 273 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
The Nasdaq Composite index, however, was off only 0.47 to 1,299.90 after Tuesday's record finish of 1,300.37, which was its seventh consecutive record and its first close above 1,300.
"This seems to be indicative of investors moving some money out of the "nifty-fifty" style stocks," said Michael LaTronica, director of research at Gruntal & Co.

While some of the stock mutual funds appeared to be loading up on secondary stocks, LaTronica said, "it's a little early to tell whether this is going to carry forward. Some of this money may be sitting on the sidelines."

The session was particularly choppy, with computerized programme trading continuing to buffet stocks. In the first hour alone, the Dow fell 30 points, reversed the loss, and then tumbled more than 30 points again.
Analysts expected some backtracking in blue chips, which had staged a scorching rally since a July sell-off, leaving technology and smaller-cap stocks far behind.

"Certainly nobody expects much more out of the Dow at this point," said Chris Dickerson, an analyst at Global Market Strategists Inc. "From a technical perspective we could see Nasdaq heading up to about 1,330."
While stocks were zigzagging, the bond market was fairly steady, even after the release of the Federal Reserve's Beige Book report on the economy.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond held steady with its yield at Tuesday's close of 6.37 percent.
The Fed's report showed that the economy kept growing at a moderate pace in November, with little or no sign of near-term wage and price pressures despite strong hiring and a tight labour market.
Among individual issues, Union Carbide Corp. fell 1-1/4 to 44-3/8 after PaineWebber lowered its rating on the company's stock.
Drug stocks were lower on profit-taking. Pfizer Inc. fell 2-1/4 to 83-3/8, Bristol Myers-Squibb Co. lost 1-7/8 to 113-3/8 and Eli Lilly & Co. shed 2-1/8 to 73-3/4.
Forest Laboratories Inc. tumbled 9-1/8 to 29-5/8 after the company warned that it expected operating losses for the next two quarters and for all of fiscal 1997.

Geotek Communications Inc. climbed 1-3/4 to 8-3/4 after the company announced a wireless voice and data services marketing agreement with International Business Machines Corp., which was up 7/8 to 163-1/2.
